steps.prompt: Which one hits harder at the end of a scary story? Why?
steps.a: The door, which had been locked for years, slowly began to open while we watched from the stairs.
steps.reveal: B is a simple sentence: one subject, one verb, one complete thought. Simple doesn’t mean babyish. Short simple sentences land like a drumbeat, which is why writers save them for big moments.

cards.title: What makes a sentence simple?
cards.body: A simple sentence has one independent clause: one subject–verb pair that makes a complete thought. “Dogs bark.” is simple. So is “The scruffy dog next door barks at every passing car.”

cards.title: Simple can still be long
cards.text:
Compound subject: Maya and Leo built a robot.
Compound predicate: The robot beeped and rolled away.
Phrases: After lunch, the robot rolled across the gym floor.
cards.note: Two subjects sharing one verb, or one subject doing two things, is still one clause. Phrases (after lunch, across the gym floor) add detail without adding a clause.

cards.title: When to use them
cards.body: Use simple sentences for your clearest points: a claim, a key fact, a turning point. In an essay, “Homework should be optional.” is a strong simple sentence.

prompts: Why can a long sentence still be simple? Use one of your sentences to explain.
Where in an essay would a short simple sentence work best?
